source.title: From Data Statistics to Feature Geometry: How Correlations Shape Superposition
source.authors: Lucas Prieto; Edward Stevinson; Melih Barsbey; Tolga Birdal; Pedro A. M. Mediano

record.tranche_reason: The study's own experiments refine the superposition account: correlated features can use interference constructively, and feature geometry varies with bottleneck size and weight decay.
record.gate_note: The paper tests superposition in synthetic and BOWS autoencoders and reports related structure in a toy transformer. It does not test individual neurons' responses to unrelated inputs. It does not test language-model neuron polysemanticity rates or improved explanations of canonical neurons. Cited claims about other models are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The study takes the superposition framework of Elhage et al. as given and studies how correlations shape feature geometry in tied-weight autoencoders (BOWS), plus a toy transformer. Its hidden layer is a linear bottleneck with no privileged neuron basis. No neuron's response to unrelated inputs is measured, and no count or share of polysemantic neurons is reported. Its refinement says interference can be constructive, but that concerns superposition geometry, not whether superposition causes polysemantic neurons (V3). Latent-size and weight-decay effects concern feature geometry, not the share of polysemantic neurons (V5). The construct is related but different, so the findings go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is essentially correct. The authors conclude that, with correlated features, superposition can use constructive interference by arranging features by co-activation. This yields norm- and rank-efficient reconstructions and explains semantic clusters and cyclical structures seen in language models. Such solutions are favoured by tight bottlenecks and weight decay. They separate these correlation-driven structures from value-coding feature manifolds that arise for functional reasons, and note that BOWS is a simplified setting.
record.recipe_differences: Introduces BOWS and studies feature geometry in synthetic and text-trained autoencoders, rather than reproducing the original neuron-interpretability method.
record.method_sensitivity: Latent size changes whether learned features show circular, antipodal, clustered, or near-orthogonal geometry. Weight decay makes semantic clustering visible across a broader range of latent sizes. The paper also examines linear versus ReLU decoders in synthetic data.

fits_no_version.finding: With correlated features, interference in superposition can be constructive. ReLU AEs on BOWS arrange features by co-activation, giving semantic clusters and circular month geometry. Months are linearly decodable (R² = 0.98), and Beatles words do better in context than one-hot.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Superposed features with correlated co-activation are arranged so interference reinforces signal (linear superposition), producing semantic clusters and cyclic geometry.

fits_no_version.finding: Tight bottlenecks and weight decay favour linear-superposition solutions. Clustering weakens at m = 800 without weight decay and reappears with weight decay 4. As m grows, features move to antipodal pairs and then become orthogonal.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Superposition geometry (linear vs non-linear, clustered vs orthogonal) depends on bottleneck size and weight decay.

fits_no_version.finding: Features differ in superposition type by frequency. In the m = 800 model, 522 frequent words are in linear superposition and 4,073 in non-linear superposition. Month structure becomes orthogonal before Roman-numeral structure as m grows.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Within one model, different feature groups occupy different regimes between linear and non-linear superposition, depending on frequency and correlation.

record.problems: The main experiments use simplified bag-of-words autoencoders rather than ordinary language-model neurons; the authors explicitly say BOWS does not capture the full richness of language-model representations. Several geometry results are qualitative plots, and the study does not measure the share of polysemantic neurons in trained models.

untested.parts: No vision models or InceptionV1 neurons.
No MLP-neuron polysemanticity rates or layerwise comparison in language models.
Does not measure polysemantic neurons or link their existence to feature count exceeding neuron count. The AE latent has no privileged basis.
No test of polysemanticity arising when capacity is sufficient.
No share of polysemantic neurons measured across activation functions, architectures or regularization. Weight-decay effects are on feature geometry only.
No reassessment of canonical polysemantic neurons.
No variation of activation-range selection or explanation scoring.

missing.what: Value-coding ablations. Keeping only the value-coding subspace preserves accuracy (MAP 93.16%, key-freq 93.99%); ablating it collapses accuracy (22.43%, 3.11%).
Off-diagonal Frobenius norm of month versus Roman-numeral Gram matrices across latent sizes.
Larger context size C raises the linear-probe FVE of ReLU-AE reconstructions and lowers the effective rank of the data.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked rows to V3/V5, but no row measures neurons responding to unrelated inputs. The tied AE's hidden layer is linear, so it has no privileged neuron basis. The related-work section restates the superposition-as-cause-of-polysemanticity view (Elhage et al.) only as cited background. Not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: No image classifier or InceptionV1 neurons are examined.
No MLP-neuron polysemanticity rate or layerwise comparison in transformer language models is measured.
Tests feature superposition in toy and autoencoder settings, not whether polysemantic neurons in trained networks are caused by representing more sparse features than there are neurons.
No test of polysemanticity arising from initialization, regularization, or training noise when capacity is sufficient.

Tests latent size and weight decay, and compares ReLU and linear autoencoders in a synthetic setting. Does not test SoLU or modern convnets, nor establish that polysemanticity can be reduced without a large performance loss.
Does not use improved neuron-explanation tools to reassess canonical polysemantic neurons or estimate how often unrelated mixtures are truly present.
Does not vary activation-range selection or explanation-scoring methods to test measurement dependence.

rows.subject: Linear AE, synthetic cyclic 12-feature data
rows.operation_detail: Measured learned weight inner products WᵀW across latent sizes.
rows.measure: Weight geometry; linear AE learns projection onto the top-m principal components and the circular data structure.
rows.value: Top-m principal-component projection; circular structure in the learned geometry.
rows.note: Authors describe this as the linear-AE baseline for the ReLU-AE comparison.
rows.check: Linear-AE comparator for weight geometry; no neuron polysemanticity measured. Not linked to V3/V5.

rows.subject: ReLU AE, synthetic cyclic 12-feature data
rows.operation_detail: Measured learned weight inner products WᵀW across latent sizes.
rows.measure: Weight geometry relative to the circular covariance structure.
rows.baseline: Linear AE projection onto top-m principal components
rows.value: ReLU AE recovers the circular structure dictated by the top principal components.
rows.note: The paper describes this range collectively; Figure 2 shows individual latent sizes.
rows.check: Feature geometry (circular PCA structure) in a toy AE with no privileged neuron basis; not a measure of polysemantic neurons.

rows.subject: ReLU AE, synthetic cyclic 12-feature data
rows.operation_detail: Measured learned weight inner products WᵀW across latent sizes.
rows.measure: Feature arrangement in the learned weights.
rows.baseline: Circular PCA-like structure at smaller latent sizes
rows.value: The AE abandons the circular PCA structure and represents features as antipodal pairs.
rows.note: Authors describe this as nonlinear superposition, with ReLU filtering negative interference.
rows.check: Antipodal-pair feature geometry; superposition geometry, not neuron polysemanticity or its cause.

rows.subject: ReLU AE, synthetic cyclic 12-feature data
rows.operation_detail: Measured learned weight geometry as latent size approaches input size.
rows.measure: Orthogonality of feature representations and retention of circular covariance structure.
rows.baseline: Circular structure at smaller latent sizes
rows.value: Weights converge to identity; features are orthogonal and the circular covariance structure is no longer reflected in the weights.
rows.note: The paper says the notion of superposition is lost as reconstruction becomes perfect.
rows.check: The 'absent' state was relative to V3/V5. The finding itself, weights converging to identity at m = 12, is observed as stated; it concerns feature geometry only.

relation.reason: Builds on the Elhage et al. superposition framework without testing neuron polysemanticity. The reader's tests/T5 call is not supported, because the study tests feature geometry, not any of V1-V7.

tranche.reason: Takes superposition as given and reports only its own BOWS feature-geometry results. No neuron polysemanticity is measured (T6 is also defensible).

source_check.notes: All rows concern feature geometry in tied-weight AEs with no privileged neuron basis, plus a toy transformer. Polysemantic neurons appear only in related work, so no verdicts are warranted. In r14, the Figure 12 caption says days of the week while the body says months. For r10, the text cites an 'm = 800 model used in Figure 9', but the extracted Figure 9 panels list m = 200/400/600/1000.
